plan: Ten new SAT R&W items across all four domains: belated (WIC), urban bird-song inference (evidence ruling out an alternative), library-hours data (shift vs new visits), records-vs-excavation cross-text, glass-sponge text structure, plural without apostrophe, sentence boundary, "the number of" agreement, contrast transition, before-and-after synthesis (Erie Canal). Topics checked against the live bank. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A reluctant witness
passages.text: In the novel's final chapter, the narrator, who has spent the book insisting that she saw nothing on the night of the fire, finally admits to having noticed a light in the barn. Her confession is ______: she offers it only after the other characters have already pieced together what happened, so it changes nothing about the outcome.

passages.title: Bird song in cities
passages.text: Researchers recording great tits in European cities found that urban males sang at higher minimum pitches than males of the same species in nearby forests. Low-pitched city noise from traffic overlaps with the lower part of the birds' songs. Some researchers have proposed that singing higher helps urban males be heard over the noise. Others have suggested that the difference reflects something else about city birds, such as their smaller body size. The finding that would most directly support the first explanation is one showing that ______

passages.title: Library visits
passages.text:
A town librarian compared monthly in-person visits before and after the library extended its weekday hours from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Before the change: 4,200 visits per month, 600 of them after 5 p.m.
After the change: 4,900 visits per month, 1,400 of them after 5 p.m.
The librarian claims that the longer hours attracted new evening visits rather than simply shifting existing visitors from earlier in the day.

passages.title: Two kinds of evidence
passages.text:
Text 1
For much of the twentieth century, historians of medieval villages relied mainly on written records such as tax rolls and court documents. These sources, one historian argues, give the most reliable picture of village life, because they record names, amounts, and dates.

Text 2
Archaeologist Rhea Moss points out that written records were produced by officials and describe mainly what officials cared about: taxes owed and crimes punished. Excavations of village houses, she notes, reveal what people actually ate, how they built their homes, and which goods they traded—matters the records rarely mention. Moss does not dismiss written sources, but she argues that neither kind of evidence is complete without the other.

passages.title: Glass sponges
passages.text: Venus's flower basket, a deep-sea sponge, builds its skeleton from fine strands of silica glass. Engineers studying the skeleton found that its lattice of crossing strands, reinforced by diagonal struts, resists bending far better than a lattice of the same mass without the diagonals. The researchers suggested that the sponge's design could guide the construction of lightweight towers and bridges.

passages.title: A coded diary
passages.text: Historians long assumed that the small diary, written in an unfamiliar shorthand, contained only household accounts. When a graduate student finally deciphered the shorthand in 2019, she discovered ______ entries describing the writer's work as a messenger during the war.

passages.title: Measuring a glacier
passages.text: To measure how fast the glacier was moving, the team drove stakes into the ice in a straight line across its ______ year later, they surveyed the stakes again and found that the line had bent into a curve, with the stakes near the center having moved farthest.

passages.title: A busy street
passages.text: The number of cyclists using the new bridge, according to counts taken by the city's transportation office over the first three months, ______ steadily each week.

passages.title: A careful conclusion
passages.text: Early studies suggested that a certain herb reduced the length of common colds. ______ later studies with larger groups and with participants who did not know whether they were taking the herb or a placebo found no difference in how long colds lasted.

passages.title: Notes on a canal
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Erie Canal opened in New York State in 1825.
- It connected the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo.
- Before the canal, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City could cost about $100.
- After the canal opened, the cost fell to roughly $10 per ton.
- New York City soon became the busiest port in the United States.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: only after the other characters have already pieced together what happened
candidates.explanation: A confession that comes after everyone has already figured things out, and changes nothing, is "belated."

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the confession required courage; the text stresses that it came too late to matter.

B.rationale: The text presents the confession as true, not invented.

C.rationale: The confession is clear (she noticed a light); its problem is timing.

hints: What does the text say about when the confession comes?
candidates.remember: Use the explanation after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: city great tits are, on average, slightly smaller than forest great tits.
choices.B: individual males in the city raise the minimum pitch of their songs on days when traffic noise is louder.
choices.C: forest great tits sing more often in the early morning than city great tits do.
choices.D: great tits in both cities and forests sing songs with several distinct notes.

candidates.evidence: singing higher helps urban males be heard over the noise
candidates.explanation: If the same birds raise their pitch when noise rises, body size cannot explain the change, which supports the idea that birds sing higher to be heard over noise.

A.rationale: This supports the alternative explanation (body size), not the noise explanation.

C.rationale: How often birds sing does not address why their pitch differs.

D.rationale: This describes a shared feature, not a cause of the pitch difference.

hints: Which finding rules out body size as the cause?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result in which noise changes but the birds do not.

candidates.remember: The best support for one explanation rules out the competing one.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the librarian's claim?

choices.A: Visits after 5 p.m. more than doubled, rising from 600 to 1,400 per month.
choices.B: Total visits rose from 4,200 to 4,900 per month after the library extended its hours.
choices.C: Evening visits rose by 800, while daytime visits fell by only 100.
choices.D: Visits before 5 p.m. remained the largest share of visits both before and after the change.

candidates.evidence: attracted new evening visits rather than simply shifting existing visitors
candidates.explanation: Daytime visits went from 3,600 to 3,500, a drop of only 100, while evening visits rose by 800. If visitors had merely shifted, daytime visits would have fallen by about as much as evening visits rose.

A.rationale: A rise in evening visits alone could come from people shifting from earlier hours; this choice does not address daytime visits.

B.rationale: This shows total growth but not that the growth came from evening visits.

D.rationale: This is true but does not show that the new evening visits were new rather than shifted.

hints: What would the data look like if visitors had only shifted?

strategy.explanation: Compute the change in daytime and evening visits separately.

candidates.remember: To rule out a shift, show that one group grew more than the other shrank.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Moss (Text 2) most likely respond to the historian's claim in Text 1?

choices.A: She would grant that records are precise but say they omit much that excavation reveals.
choices.B: She would argue that written records are unreliable and should no longer be used by historians.
choices.C: She would agree that written records alone give the most reliable picture of village life.
choices.D: She would argue that excavations reveal more names, amounts, and dates than written records do.

candidates.evidence: neither kind of evidence is complete without the other
candidates.explanation: Moss accepts that records have value but says they mainly reflect officials' concerns; excavation supplies what they leave out.

B.rationale: Moss explicitly does not dismiss written sources.

C.rationale: Moss argues that neither kind of evidence is complete without the other.

D.rationale: Moss says excavations reveal diet, building and trade, not names and amounts.

hints: Does Moss reject written records, or say they are incomplete?

strategy.explanation: Separate what Moss grants from what she disputes.

candidates.remember: Watch for a position that qualifies, rather than rejects, another.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a debate among engineers and then explains which side the evidence favors.
choices.B: It explains how sponges make glass and then compares their method with industrial glassmaking.
choices.C: It describes a natural structure, reports a finding about it, and notes a possible use.
choices.D: It describes a problem in bridge design and then explains how sponges cause that problem.

candidates.evidence: could guide the construction of lightweight towers and bridges
candidates.explanation: The text introduces the sponge's glass skeleton, reports that its diagonal struts make it resist bending, and ends with a suggested engineering use.

B.rationale: The text does not explain how sponges make glass or discuss industry.

D.rationale: The sponge is a model for design, not the cause of a problem.

hints: What does each sentence of the text do?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence, then match the sequence.

candidates.remember: Describe structure by the job each part does.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "Dozens of entries" uses the plural noun "dozens" with no apostrophe.

A.rationale: An apostrophe is not used to make "dozen" plural.

C.rationale: No possession is involved, so no apostrophe is needed.

D.rationale: "Dozen of entries" is not standard; the plural "dozens of" is needed.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses are correctly separated by a period.

B.rationale: A comma alone cannot join the two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

hints: How many independent clauses are there?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Two independent clauses need a period, a semicolon, or a comma with a conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The number of cyclists using the new bridge
candidates.explanation: The subject is "The number," which is singular, so the verb must be singular. "Rose" works for a singular subject and fits the past-tense context of the counts.

A.rationale: The subject is "number," which is singular; "have" is plural.

B.rationale: "Were" is plural and disagrees with the singular subject "number."

D.rationale: "Are" is plural and disagrees with "number"; it also shifts to the present tense.

hints: What is the subject of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrases between the subject and the verb.

candidates.remember: "The number of" takes a singular verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: found no difference in how long colds lasted
candidates.explanation: The later studies contradicted the early suggestion, so a contrast transition fits.

A.rationale: The later studies contradict the early ones; they are not similar.

B.rationale: The later studies do not illustrate the early claim.

C.rationale: The early studies did not cause the later results.

hints: Do the later studies agree or disagree with the early ones?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use a contrast transition when later evidence contradicts earlier evidence.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much the canal reduced shipping costs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Erie Canal, which opened in 1825, connected the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo.
choices.B: The Erie Canal cut the cost of shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City from about $100 to roughly $10.
choices.C: After the Erie Canal opened, New York City soon became the busiest port in the United States.
choices.D: Before the canal, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City could cost about $100.

candidates.evidence: the cost fell to roughly $10 per ton
candidates.explanation: Emphasizing the reduction requires both the before and after costs; only choice B gives both.

A.rationale: This describes the route, not the change in shipping costs.

C.rationale: This states a consequence, not the size of the cost reduction.

D.rationale: This gives only the earlier cost, so it cannot show how much costs fell.

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: To show a change, include both the before and after values.
